verdicts.trueWording: DMs found that the model struggled sometimes to describe combat
verdicts.note: ar5iv 2308.07540 fetched raw (HTTP 200). One sentence carries every limb: 'DMs found that the model struggled sometimes to describe combat, and suggested that including more information about the combat state ... or map placement information could help generate more specific descriptions (P3, P9). Some DMs used these descriptions verbatim (P3, P8, P17), while others picked out particularly vivid phrases to use in a description of their own (P3, P8, P10, P12, P20). Others disagreed with the model's description and wrote their own instead (P13, P16, P18, P19).' Three-way split confirmed with participant ids. Minor framing note: the missing combat-state/map-placement is the DMs' suggested remedy, so the causal 'because' is the paper's implication rather than its assertion.

verdicts.trueWording: no helpful summary when a monster had only numeric game stats
verdicts.note: No quote was supplied, so substance-graded. Page: 'Another common case where Calypso did not present a helpful summary was when a monster did not have a published prose description, only numeric game stats. Most commonly, such creatures were an animal found in real life (e.g. a brown bear; P3) or relied entirely on a DM's thematic commonsense to run (e.g. a snow golem; P3).' The remedy limb is explicit: 'we had to prompt it with explicit instructions to do so ... we remodeled the summarization task to a more abstract "understanding" task, in which we provided the model explicit instructions to use thematic commonsense.' One softening: the paper says the model used 'minimal external knowledge', not literally nothing to draw on.

verdicts.trueWording: different users tended to produce less semantically distinct ideas with ChatGPT
verdicts.note: arxiv 2402.01536 HTML fetched raw. Abstract carries the quote verbatim and the 36-participant within-subjects design; Section 3.2.2 confirms the Oblique Strategies deck as comparator. p-value exact: 'M = .24, SD = .07 ... compared to ... OS, (M = .28, SD = .08), t(32) = 2.154, p = 0.038, d = .47' followed by 'At the group level, ideas produced with the help of ChatGPT were more homogenized.' Individual-level null confirmed separately (t(32) = .944, p = 0.352) and the discussion states homogenization 'stems not from individual-level increases in fixation ... but from group-level suggestion of similar ideas to different users by the LLM.' Note 36 were recruited, 3 excluded, so tests run at df=32.

verdicts.trueWording: When I asked for more [ChatGPT] repeated half
verdicts.note: Quote appears verbatim twice: in the participant-quote table ('When I asked for more [ChatGPT] repeated half... When I want more, I want different more.') and in the discussion ('"When I want more", one user asserts, "I want different more."'). Plural-participant limb supported: 'a few ChatGPT users explicitly noted the repetitiveness of the model's responses' and the interview theme 'the LLM responses were too repetitive (8.33%, n = 3)'.

verdicts.trueWording: single most common theme was ChatGPT easier to use but less rewarding
verdicts.note: Section 4.4.1 is headed 'Interview', so the 'interview theme' limb is exact. Page: 'The single most common theme was that ChatGPT was easier to use but less rewarding (27.78%, n = 10). ... Participants also reported finding ChatGPT to be less engaging (22.22%, n =8)'. Both counts match the claim.

verdicts.trueWording: attributable in part to the low inferential distance between LLM outputs and apparently complete ideas
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim in three places; the takeaway sentence matches the claim's exact phrasing: 'we suggest that the homogenization effect of LLMs on creative ideation is attributable in part to the low inferential distance between LLM outputs and apparently complete ideas.' The gloss 'arrives looking finished, so users stop diverging' is supported by Section 5.2: low inferential distance 'can be viewed as enabling algorithmic loafing ... simply accepting and passing along the decisions made by the algorithm', versus OS cards where the user 'has to do more work to interpret the text'.

verdicts.trueWording: fifteen hundred words ... the result of at least fifteen hundred decisions
verdicts.note: PDF fetched raw (HTTP 200, 349,849 bytes) and text-extracted locally with pdfminer. Quote verbatim. The numeric limb is on the page spelled out, not in digits, which is why a digit search misses it: 'A piece of writing that contains fifteen hundred words can be thought of as the result of at least fifteen hundred decisions'. Delegation limb: authors expanding 'a one-sentence instruction' to 'a complete written story or essay ... delegate many of the creative decisions ... resulting in a piece of writing with an unusually low ratio of human decision-making to output length.'

verdicts.trueWording: The term 'soullessness' reflects the sparseness of intent in the outputs
verdicts.note: Near-word-for-word on the page: 'The term "soullessness" reflects the sparseness of intent in the outputs that are easiest to create with many AI-based tools, and that therefore dominate most non-enthusiasts' impressions'. The 'recurring verdict' limb is supported by the preceding sentence: outputs 'are often referred to as "soulless"'.

verdicts.trueWording: an ear for evocative language and a strong aversion to cliche
verdicts.note: Page: 'Experienced writers tend to have an ear for evocative language and a strong aversion to cliché ... These writers are readily able to identify problems in AI-generated text [5]'. Novice limb equally explicit: 'Novice writers, on the other hand, may tend to treat the machine as a creative authority [2] and delegate a greater proportion of their creative decisions - a form of algorithmic loafing'.

verdicts.trueWording: greater homogenization from tools that make a greater proportion of decisions directly
verdicts.note: Page: 'Homogenization effects can be explained by authors' delegation of creative decision-making to a tool that makes similar creative decisions in similar usage scenarios, with greater degrees of homogenization resulting from tools that make a greater proportion of creative decisions directly.' Both limbs, including the proportionality, are in that one sentence.

verdicts.trueWording: effective at open-domain story generation ... struggle with long-term story coherence
verdicts.note: arxiv 2406.00554 fetched raw. Page: 'LLMs, on the other hand, are effective at open-domain story generation. However, they tend to struggle with long-term story coherence, often failing to produce a satisfying overall story arc or reader experience Kreminski and Martens (2022).' Provenance caveat for citation use: this is the paper's related-work framing attributed to Kreminski and Martens 2022, not a new result measured in this paper.

verdicts.trueWording: unoriginality or homogeneity in both the semantic and syntactic aspects of generated stories
verdicts.note: Same sentence block: 'comparing LLM-generated to human-written stories reveals many aesthetic weaknesses ... in particular a tendency toward unoriginality or homogeneity in both the semantic and syntactic aspects of generated stories Anderson et al. (2024); Begus (2023).' The claim's gloss of semantic/syntactic as 'what happens / how sentences are built' is a fair rendering. Same provenance caveat: the page attributes this to Anderson et al. 2024 and Begus 2023.

verdicts.unsupportedLimb: 'openings converge hardest' - the paper immediately qualifies the trend as 'relatively weak' and says it 'did not hold across all premises', a hedge the claim drops
verdicts.trueWording: earlier paragraphs tended to be more homogenous than later paragraphs
verdicts.note: No quote was supplied. The measurable limbs check out: 'For each premise, we generated a set of ten seven-paragraph stories using each approach' (ten-story sets per premise, six premises) and 'We also observed that earlier paragraphs tended to be more homogenous than later paragraphs regardless of whether ASP guidance was used.' The very next sentence is the problem: 'However, this trend was relatively weak and did not hold across all premises.' The paper also offers a mechanism opposite in spirit to hard convergence - later paragraphs are more diverse because minor early differences 'pile up'. Graded PARTIAL because a flat superlative reading of the opening convergence is not what the page supports.

verdicts.trueWording: Existing instruction-tuned models formed one cluster ... high reward but with low diversity
verdicts.note: arxiv 2503.17126 fetched raw. All three limbs land. Quality-vs-diversity: 'proximal policy optimization (PPO) ... or direct preference optimization (DPO) ... can strongly increase the quality of LLM output, this tuning also seems to decrease output diversity.' Cluster: 'Existing instruction-tuned models (GPT-4o, GPT-4o-iter, o1, Claude-3.5-sonnet, DeepSeek-R1, Instruct) formed one cluster, where they show high reward but with low diversity.' Deviation objective: abstract states the deviation-weighted DPO/ORPO model 'could achieve on-par diversity as a human-created dataset while having output quality similar to the best instruction-tuned models'; plain DPO and ORPO by contrast raised reward 'while either maintaining or decreasing diversity', which supports the 'was needed' framing.

verdicts.unsupportedLimb: '28% for humans' for Man in Hole - Figure 4 gives the human share as 30.7% (GPT-4 51.3%); no 28% figure for that arc appears anywhere in the paper
verdicts.trueWording: Man in Hole: 30.7% of human stories versus 51.3% of GPT-4 stories
verdicts.note: HTML fetched raw, then the arXiv PDF fetched and text-extracted because the arc shares live only in the Figure 4 pie charts, whose labels survive as vector text in the PDF. Legend order 'Oedipus, Cinderella, Riches to Rags, Rags to Riches, Icarus, Man in Hole, Double Man in Hole' against human '9.3% 15.1% 14.6% 4.4% 4.9% 30.7% 21.0%' and GPT-4 '1.7% 17.2% 1.3% 13.0% 2.9% 51.3% 12.6%'. The mapping is cross-checked by four figures stated in prose (Oedipus 9.3/1.7, Riches to Rags 14.6/1.3, Rags to Riches 4.4/13.0), so Man in Hole is 30.7% human, 51.3% GPT-4. Everything else verifies: the quote is verbatim in the abstract; the corpus is 819 human synopses with one paired GPT-4 synopsis each (1638 total); 'more than half of the time' matches 'over 50%'; and Riches to Rags 1.3% vs 14.6% is exact. Only the human Man in Hole figure is wrong - it should read roughly 31%, not 28%.
